headline: Two teams switch on the first nuclear clocks
summary: Two independent teams (TU Wien/PTB and Tsinghua) demonstrate operating thorium-229 nuclear clocks in Nature, one already constraining ultralight dark matter.
display_body: Every precision clock works the same way. A laser's frequency drifts, so it is locked to something in nature that only responds to one exact frequency. Today's best clocks use electrons jumping between energy levels in atoms. A nuclear clock uses the atom's nucleus instead. The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller and far better shielded, so it should be much less disturbed by stray electric and magnetic fields. Almost every nucleus needs far too much energy for a laser to flip it. The single known exception is thorium-229, whose transition sits at 148 nm (vacuum ultraviolet). Since the 2024 papers that first excited it with a laser, the open question has been whether anyone could close the loop and actually run a clock on it. This week two independent groups did. Both embed thorium-229 in a small calcium-fluoride crystal and lock a continuous-wave 148-nm laser to the nuclear resonance by measuring how much light the crystal absorbs. The Vienna-led team, with Germany's national metrology institute PTB, reports a fractional instability (how much the tick wanders, relative to its frequency) of 3×10⁻¹²/√τ, approaching 10⁻¹⁵ over a day. They checked it continuously against PTB's ytterbium-ion clock. The Tsinghua team reaches 5×10⁻¹³/√τ, and shows that two separately grown crystals tick at the same frequency to within 10⁻¹³, the reproducibility a practical standard needs. Both clocks are still well short of the best atomic clocks, which reach the 10⁻¹⁸ level. The Vienna group projects improvements of several orders of magnitude.
why: The Vienna team has already used its clock as an instrument. A search for "ultralight dark matter" (a hypothetical field that would make the nuclear transition energy wobble) found no signal. The resulting limits match the best atomic clocks for dark matter coupling to light and go beyond previous measurements for coupling to the strong force. This is a milestone for European metrology, led from Vienna and Braunschweig.

headline: Topological probe reads an altermagnet's spins
summary: Helical edge modes of a topological insulator used as an STM spin probe reveal 2D d-wave altermagnetic order on KV2Se2O.
display_body: Altermagnets are a recently recognised third class of magnet. Like antiferromagnets, they have zero net magnetisation because neighbouring spins cancel. Like ferromagnets, their electrons still split into spin-up and spin-down bands, with a sign that alternates by direction in the crystal (a "d-wave" pattern, like a four-leaf clover with alternating colours). Proving that a material really is one requires seeing spin both on the atomic lattice and in momentum space, and nobody had done both. The team turned a scanning-tunnelling-microscope tip into a spin detector by picking up a flake of α-Bi₄Br₄. This is a higher-order topological insulator whose edges carry "helical" channels, where electrons moving one way all have the same spin. On the surface layer of KV₂Se₂O they mapped the two vanadium sublattices and a checkerboard antiferromagnetic pattern. In momentum space they found opposite spin responses in the two symmetry-paired valleys (X and Y) that flip when the bias is reversed. That is the d-wave signature.
why: Altermagnets are attractive for spintronics because they could carry spin-polarised currents without stray magnetic fields. This gives the field a direct atomic-scale test for confirming candidate materials. The authors present it as "converging evidence" rather than a single decisive measurement.

headline: Iron catalyst makes polyethylene's surface sticky
summary: Iron-catalysed C-H oxidation at the solid-liquid interface adds ketones only to polyethylene surfaces, raising adhesion up to 90-fold.
display_body: Polyethylene is more than a quarter of all plastic made. Its chemical inertness is the reason it is useful, and also the reason glue, paint and ink don't stick to it. Adding polar chemical groups helps, but doing it throughout the material degrades the bulk properties manufacturers rely on. John Hartwig's group instead runs the reaction at the solid–liquid interface, so only the surface of solid polyethylene reacts. With 0.001 mol% of an iron catalyst, cheap oxidants and temperatures below 80 °C, they selectively convert CH₂ units to ketones (C=O groups). Melting point and tensile strength are unchanged. The treated plastic bonds to polar surfaces up to 90 times more strongly than untreated polyethylene, and up to four times more strongly than polyethylene functionalised in solution to a similar level. The effect also lasts longer than it does after conventional unselective surface treatments.
why: Plastics that adhere better are easier to laminate, print and combine with other materials. The result is lab-scale; the open question is whether a dilute iron catalyst can be made to work on industrial lines.

headline: Iodide unlocks a reversible tin battery anode
summary: Iodide complexes make Sn4+/Sn2+ reversible, enabling a four-electron tin flow-battery anode and a kW stack running 1,000 hours.
display_body: Flow batteries store energy in liquids pumped through a cell and are a candidate for grid storage. Tin is attractive for the negative side because each ion can in principle carry four electrons (Sn⁴⁺ to Sn⁰) and it does not grow dendrites, the metal spikes that short-circuit many batteries. In practice the Sn⁴⁺/Sn²⁺ step has been irreversible. Adding iodide to concentrated SnCl₄ forms SnI₆²⁻ complexes, which lower the energy cost of rearranging the ion during electron transfer. The gap between charge and discharge peak potentials falls from 978 mV to 97 mV, while chloride complexes keep the tin dissolved. Paired with a bromine positive side, a cell reached 89% energy efficiency at 40 mA cm⁻² and 205 Wh per litre of anolyte. A kilowatt-scale stack ran stably for over 1,000 hours.
why: Energy per litre is the weak point of aqueous flow batteries. A kilowatt-scale stack running for 1,000 hours is a step beyond the usual coin-cell demonstration, though bromine handling remains a practical cost.

headline: Optogenetic sight therapy passes ten-patient test
summary: NEJM trial of ChrimsonR optogenetic gene therapy with goggles in 10 retinitis pigmentosa patients finds it safe with modest gains in six.
display_body: In retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited disease caused by mutations in any of hundreds of genes, the light-sensing rods and cones die. The retinal ganglion cells that send signals to the brain often survive. Optogenetics, which won this month's medicine Nobel, can make those surviving cells light-sensitive. In 2021 the Sahel/Roska team reported partial vision in a single patient. This trial treated 10 patients with advanced disease, each in the worse-seeing eye. They received a gene for ChrimsonR, a light-gated channel that responds to amber (~590 nm) light, at one of three doses. Special goggles turn camera images into pulses of amber light projected onto the retina. The primary endpoint was safety. There were 33 mild-to-moderate eye events in nine patients, such as transient inflammation and raised eye pressure, plus one severe event that resolved within minutes. Light sensitivity rose 2- to 62-fold in seven of ten patients, a clinically meaningful amount in six. Several did better at finding and touching objects with the goggles. EEG (scalp brain-recording) decoding improved with the goggles when the eyes were open but not when closed, which suggests a real visual signal rather than an artefact. Patients who trained longer did better. All the reports, the institute's included, stress that normal sight was not restored, and ten patients is too few to characterise response well.
why: This moves optogenetic sight restoration from one case to a cohort. Because it bypasses the faulty gene, it could in principle work for any form of the disease. The work is co-led from Basel's Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology, where Botond Roska's group designed the approach.

headline: Bacterial defence enzyme works like telomerase
summary: Defence reverse transcriptase DRT10 synthesises tandem DNA repeats with telomerase-like logic; phylogeny places telomerase within the DRT family.
display_body: Bacteria carry a wide range of anti-phage defences, among them "defence-associated reverse transcriptases" (DRTs). These enzymes write DNA from an RNA template, the reverse of the usual flow, and many of their mechanisms are still unknown. Samuel Sternberg's lab characterised DRT10. It binds a non-coding RNA and, starting from a protein primer, writes long stretches of DNA made of the same short sequence repeated over and over. Cryo-EM (frozen-sample electron microscopy) shows an unexpected structure: two enzyme copies clamp opposite faces of a roughly symmetric RNA. Only one copy makes the long repeat. Its length is set by two stem-loop "anchors" on the RNA that mark the template's boundaries. That boundary-limited, repeat-after-repeat copying is how telomerase works. Telomerase is the eukaryotic enzyme that rebuilds chromosome ends. An evolutionary tree of reverse transcriptases from all domains of life places telomerase in the same branch as the DRT family.
why: Telomerase is central to ageing and cancer biology, and its evolutionary origin has been unclear. This points to a bacterial immune system as its likely ancestor. The shared-origin claim rests on phylogenetics and is an inference, not a demonstration.

headline: Menopause hits as a cliff, not a slope
summary: Reconstruction from 300 million lab tests shows a step-like multisystem shift at the final menstrual period, attenuated with hormone therapy.
display_body: Menopause is usually described as a gradual transition, based on small cohorts followed over years. Big medical databases rarely record the age of the final menstrual period (FMP), so averaging women by age blurs any sharp change, because FMP age varies by a decade or more. Uri Alon's group borrowed an idea from astronomy: deblurring. They mathematically remove the spread in FMP age to reconstruct trajectories anchored on the FMP itself from cross-sectional data, meaning one snapshot per person rather than repeated measurements. Across two independent cohorts totalling 300 million laboratory tests, they find a step-like jump at the FMP in hormonal, bone, liver, kidney and lipid markers. The step is absent in men and consistent across populations. It appears much smaller in women on menopausal hormone therapy, though that is an observational comparison, not a trial. Hormonal changes start more than a decade before the FMP.
why: If menopause is an abrupt, body-wide shift, then monitoring and the timing of treatment around the FMP deserve more attention than a "gradual decline" view suggests. The deblurring method could also be applied to other hidden transitions, such as puberty.

headline: Personal ovarian cancer vaccine proves feasible
summary: Phase 1 NeoVax neoantigen vaccine trial in ovarian cancer is safe and feasible at recurrence, with biomarker activity in six of ten.
display_body: Neoantigens are protein fragments that exist only in a patient's tumour because of its mutations, which makes them targets for a custom vaccine. This phase 1 trial (a small first-in-human safety and feasibility study) tested Dana-Farber's "NeoVax". It consists of patient-specific synthetic peptides mixed with an immune stimulant (poly-ICLC), followed later by an anti-PD-1 checkpoint antibody. Patients had high-grade ovarian cancer that responded to platinum chemotherapy. Ten were vaccinated. Feasibility was the sticking point: 9 of 12 evaluable patients at first recurrence received a vaccine, but only 1 of 9 newly diagnosed patients did. There were no unexpected safety signals. More than 70% of the chosen targets were still detectable in blood-borne tumour DNA a median 6.5 months after biopsy. Biomarkers suggested vaccine activity in six of ten patients.
why: Ovarian cancer usually recurs after chemotherapy, so a personalised maintenance option would matter. This is a ten-patient feasibility study with no efficacy readout, and the manufacturing lag still excludes most newly diagnosed patients.

headline: Solar Orbiter traces switchbacks to coronal loops
summary: Heavy-ion composition inside a magnetic switchback measured by Solar Orbiter ties it to hot closed coronal loops and interchange reconnection.
display_body: "Switchbacks" are sharp S-shaped kinks in the magnetic field of the solar wind, the stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun. Parker Solar Probe found them everywhere close to the Sun, but where they form has been debated. Using ESA's Solar Orbiter at 0.55 AU (a bit over half the Earth–Sun distance), the team measured heavy ions inside one large switchback. Oxygen and carbon were in unusually high charge states, meaning more electrons stripped off, and helium was depleted relative to protons. Those are fingerprints of plasma that was cooked in hot, closed magnetic loops in the corona (the Sun's outer atmosphere). A coronal model constrained by Solar Dynamics Observatory data traces the source to the edge of a coronal hole or loops inside one. That points to interchange reconnection: closed loops snap onto open field lines and fling plasma out. The kink's motion matches an outward-travelling Alfvén wave (a magnetic wave along the field). The authors conclude that reconnection creates switchbacks and waves or turbulence carry them outward. This is one well-measured event, not a statistical sample.
why: Switchbacks keep a chemical record of where they came from, so they can be used to probe how the corona is heated and the solar wind accelerated, two long-standing puzzles. The result comes from a European-led mission, and its author list is largely European.

headline: JWST maps a hot Jupiter's whole limb
summary: Transmission strings mapping of WASP-17 b with JWST reveals a ~650 K morning-evening temperature contrast around the limb.
display_body: When a planet crosses its star, starlight filters through the thin ring of atmosphere at its edge (the "limb"). Usually that whole ring is averaged into a single spectrum. Using a new "transmission strings" mapping technique on JWST data from 0.6 to 12 µm, the team split WASP-17 b's limb by angle, from east to west and from equator to pole. The morning side comes out at about 858 K and the evening side at about 1,522 K, a difference of roughly 650 K. That is consistent with the planet's separately measured dayside and nightside maps. Water and CO₂ abundances look constant around the limb.
why: This is one of the most complete 3D pictures of any exoplanet's atmosphere, and it gives direct tests for the climate models used to interpret every hot-Jupiter spectrum. The morning-side temperature carries wide error bars (+434/−233 K).

headline: Planetary systems split into two families
summary: Multi-planet systems show a bimodal mass split: calm packed low-mass systems and dynamically hot high-mass systems around metal-rich stars.
display_body: With over a thousand known multi-planet systems, the team defined metrics that work regardless of a system's layout and applied them to four independently selected samples. System masses split into two groups. The lower-mass family orbits stars from somewhat smaller than the Sun to Sun-like. Its planets are tightly packed and similar in size ("peas in a pod"), and their orbits are about as calm as the Solar System's. The high-mass family forms around metal-rich, Sun-like or larger stars. It is gravitationally compact but about ten times "hotter" dynamically (more eccentric and inclined orbits), which suggests a past of instabilities and planets scattering each other.
why: The split suggests a star's mass and chemistry steer which kind of planetary system forms. Observational bias against Solar-System-like systems still limits how far this can be generalised. Most of the team is European, led from Italy's INAF.

headline: Hint of an early reionization burst
summary: Preprint finds a 2-2.5 sigma preference in CMB data for a brief burst of reionization at redshift ~45-165.
display_body: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) records how many free electrons the early universe had. Its "optical depth" τ measures how much CMB light was scattered on the way. The standard story is that the first galaxies ionised (reionised) hydrogen late, below redshift ~15. This paper tests an alternative: unusually dense small-scale clumps collapsed very early, around redshift ~100, and briefly formed stars or black holes that ionised gas before it recombined. Fitting a wide range of cosmological data, the authors find a 2–2.5σ preference for a short-lived burst adding Δτ ≈ 0.012, the same answer under both main Planck data reprocessings. The inferred epoch depends on which reprocessing is used, ranging from redshift ~45 to ~165.
why: A significance of 2–2.5σ is a hint, not a detection, and the shifting epoch is a warning sign. The test is concrete, though: the authors say Japan's planned LiteBIRD satellite should detect such a burst and the Simons Observatory should constrain it.
